newsitem.title: THAILAND: Clinton ends Asia trip, seeks fight on drugs, AIDS.
newsitem.headline: Clinton ends Asia trip, seeks fight on drugs, AIDS.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton called on Tuesday for a deeper partnership throughout Asia and the Pacific to deal with spreading "forces of destruction" like AIDS and illegal drugs.

In a speech summarising a lengthy trip that included stops in Australia and the Philippines and private talks with the leaders of China, Japan and South Korea, Clinton praised the economic progress made in the Pacific Rim but said many daunting tasks remain.
"We must deepen our partnership for the demands of the 21st century," Clinton said in a speech at Bangkok's Chulalongkorn University, where several thousand people waited outside to cheer him.

"For all its promise, the 21st century will not be free of peril," said Clinton, speaking at the university where President Lyndon Johnson addressed students 30 years ago during the height of the Vietnam War.

Citing such problems as environmental threats, AIDS, drug trafficking and the rise of organised crime, Clinton warned that "no nation is immune to the forces of destruction and none can defeat these threats alone. Therefore we must work together."
Clinton singled out Burma for criticism, saying it "has long been the world's number one producer of opium and heroin and now is also making metamphetamines."

"The role of drugs in Burma's economic and political life and the regime's refusal to honour its own pledge to move to multiparty democracy are really two sides of the same coin, for both represent the absence of the rule of law," Clinton said.

Clinton, who arrived in Thailand on Monday night following a summit in the Philippines of the leaders of the 18-member Asian-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, praised the group's final declaration as an example of the spirit that drives the region heading into the next century.

He met privately with outgoing prime minister Banharn Silpa-archa and with the Thai premier's successor, Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, whose New Aspiration Party won a slim victory in the country's November 17 election.
During his speech, Clinton praised the democratic process in Thailand, calling this month's elections a "milestone in your democratic journey."

Noting that he had himself experienced victory and defeat at the hands of voters, Clinton said that "while losing is not as good as winning, whenever power is transferred peacefully and democratically, everyone in that nation is a winner."
Chavalit, a general and former Thai army chief, said in an interview with Reuters that he thanked Clinton for his public remarks about the peaceful transition in Thailand.
"We discussed details on how to expand our friendship ... and trade and investments," Chavalit said, adding that he was impressed by Clinton's warmth.

Clinton and his wife Hillary spent part of the day as tourists, visiting the Temple of the Emerald Buddha, a magnificent gilded structure with a sloping roof of red and green tile. They were led on their tour by Prince Subhadris.

Earlier, at an outdoor ceremony, Clinton witnessed the signing of a tax treaty between the two nations that eliminates double taxation on the earnings of U.S. firms operating in Thailand and on their counterparts in the United States.
Clinton and his wife, who made a separate visit to northern Thailand on Sunday and Monday, were to return to Washington on Wednesday.
